newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Below noise of war, hope of Afghan peace.
newsitem.headline: Below noise of war, hope of Afghan peace.

text.p: Below the noise of war and the clamour of threat and counter-threat in Afghanistan, there may just possibly be an opportunity for rival claimants to power to negotiate a peace, Afghan watchers said on Wednesday.

No one is more than mildly optimistic that the purist Islamic Taleban, which took Kabul on September 27, and a strong coalition around ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood can negotiate.
"The complications within the two sides, as well as the enmity between them, mean only the very boldest would make a prediction," one veteran Afghan watcher told Reuters.
"But, it seems in Afghanistan that as the fortunes of one side rise and those of the other fall, there is a brief point where they cross when talks are possible," he said.
"It is possible that we are nearing that point."
Two weeks ago, Masood's fortunes were at a low ebb, penned inside his Panjsher valley fortress north of Kabul after withdrawing from the city as the Taleban descended on it.

Now he has rolled back the largely ethnic Pashtun Taleban towards Kabul, has the overt backing of powerful northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum and has told the Taleban to quit the capital or face a bloodbath.

The Taleban, born two years ago in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, waved off the Masood ultimatum, saying they were strong enough to defend a city ravaged by four years of factional fighting.
They have also said a Taleban counter-attack would deliver a "tooth-breaking response" to Masood, leader of the ethnic Tajiks.
But the Afghan watchers said that their reverses, after sweeping to power in three-quarters of Afghanistan, threaten a crumbling from within.

"The Taleban hierarchy is solid, but their momentum, which seemed unstoppable, has swept up a lot of groups that might swap sides again if they feel the other side is stronger," said one. "The Taleban must be aware of the danger and it is something that might encourage them to talk."
Attempts by neighbouring Pakistan and United Nations Special envoy Norbert Holl to get the various parties to sit down and talk peace have so far come to nothing.
But there are still slim hopes.

"It's a very hard picture to read, but the feeling is that Masood isn't strong enough on his own at the moment to take Kabul and the Taleban aren't strong enough to push him back," said another Afghan watcher.
"That means Dostum could well be the key and he seems to be willing to talk as long as all the parties, including Masood, are part of them." he said.
"I find it interesting that although he has said he will support Masood, we have no evidence so far that his troops have been involved in the fighting," he added.
"All his public statements indicate that he wants to broker a peace that will give him a large say in the next government."
The Taleban position is that Masood must lay down his arms but that they are willing to talk to Dostum, who has perhaps the strongest fighting force in Afghanistan and a small air force.

He runs six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces from the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif with a liberal Islamic flavour. His men often display a fondness for vodka and women, anathema to the Taleban who have imposed Islam's stern Sharia law on Kabul.

"The fact that the Taleban are willing to talk to Dostum, despite his being a former communist and running the kind of regime they hate, must mean there is an opening for talks, if only someone could figure out where it is," said another Afghan watcher.
